claims.text: The starting material is commercial ZrB2 powder with a particle size of 1–10 µm.
The starting ZrB2 powder contains 1–2 wt % oxygen and no sintering aid.
Adding 5 wt % nano-amorphous carbon enables ZrB2 densification at approximately 2000 °C.
The carbon addition lowers the required sintering temperature by approximately 300 °C.
Amorphous carbon reduces ZrO2 films at ZrB2 particle surfaces and grain boundaries.
Carbon reacts with surface ZrO2 to produce CO and/or CO2.
Removal of surface oxides cleans grain boundaries and promotes diffusion or mass transport.
Enhanced diffusion caused by oxide removal enables full densification at a lower temperature.
Carbon-assisted lower-temperature densification reduces residual porosity and thereby improves structural integrity during prolonged liquid-plating exposure.
Carbon-doped ZrB2 will reach at least 98% theoretical density after SPS at 2000 °C for 30 minutes under 50 MPa in Ar.
Carbon-doped ZrB2 will have at least 50% less residual porosity than the conventionally prepared control.
After 500 hours in a 900 °C molten-salt plating bath, carbon-doped specimens will have less than 1% pore area fraction.
Undoped ZrB2 sintered at 2300 °C reaches approximately 95% theoretical density.
Undoped ZrB2 sintered at 2300 °C has approximately 5% residual pore volume.
After 500 hours of plating-bath exposure, the undoped control will have more than 5% pore area fraction.
The proposed preparation domain is 1800–2300 °C and 0–10 wt % carbon.
The proposed service domain is a plating bath at 800–1000 °C for exposures up to 1000 hours.
Density, open and closed porosity, post-exposure pore area fraction, and flexural strength can be used to compare the doped and undoped specimens.

The hypothesis is falsified if the doped material does not reach 98% theoretical density, reduces residual porosity by less than 30%, or has a post-bath pore area fraction at least as high as the control.
